subject: anaesthesia
title: Spine, awake craniotomy and neuromonitoring

steps.tx: For prone spine surgery the **Wilson frame** keeps the abdomen free, which reduces venous engorgement and surgical bleeding. The team protects the **eyes** carefully, pads every pressure point and positions the arms to avoid a **brachial plexus** injury. Blood loss may need transfusion support with tranexamic acid and cell salvage where available. A free abdomen also improves ventilation during a long operation.
steps.say: The patient will lie face down on a special frame for surgery on the back. The frame leaves the belly free so that veins do not become congested during surgery. Nurses pad the eyes, elbows and other pressure points before the operation begins. This careful positioning reduces bleeding and protects nerves in the arms. Good planning matters even more when the patient has severe obesity.

steps.tx: Intraoperative monitoring uses **SSEP** signals from dorsal columns and **MEP** signals from corticospinal tracts during spine surgery. Electromyography watches nerve roots and helps to check pedicle screws. Volatile agents suppress motor signals, so **total intravenous anaesthesia** with propofol and remifentanil preserves them better. A fall in amplitude warns the surgeon to pause and raise the blood pressure.
steps.say: Special recordings can watch the spinal cord while the surgeon works near it. One signal will travel through the sensory pathways at the back of the cord. Another signal tests the motor pathways that control voluntary muscle movement. Certain inhaled anaesthetics weaken the motor signal and confuse the recording team. Intravenous anaesthesia preserves the signals better and helps the team detect injury early.

steps.tx: This composite shows **SSEP** monitoring of dorsal columns and **MEP** monitoring of corticospinal tracts during spine surgery. The pump delivers **total intravenous anaesthesia** because volatile agents suppress motor signals. The soft bite block protects the tongue when motor stimulation makes the jaw clench. For the exam, link each signal with its pathway and remember that a major amplitude fall demands an immediate alert.
steps.say: The picture brings together the main parts of monitoring during spine surgery. One panel shows the sensory pathways that carry signals toward the brain. Another panel shows the motor pathways that carry commands toward the muscles. The pump gives intravenous drugs that preserve those signals better than inhaled agents. A soft block between the teeth protects the tongue when stimulation makes the jaw close.

steps.tx: In **awake craniotomy** the patient sleeps, wakes for testing and sleeps again in the asleep awake asleep technique. A **scalp block** with ropivacaine and sedation with **dexmedetomidine** keep the patient comfortable yet cooperative. The surgeon maps speech and movement so that tumour removal spares important cortex. Cold saline on the cortex can stop a seizure during mapping.
steps.say: The patient wakes during brain surgery so the surgeon can test speech and movement. Local anaesthetic blocks the scalp nerves and reduces pain from the head frame. A gentle sedative keeps the patient calm while still allowing clear conversation. The surgeon stimulates small areas and watches which function changes during testing. This mapping helps the surgeon remove tumour while sparing speech and movement.

vis.alt: Illustration of an awake patient undergoing craniotomy with a surgeon performing brain mapping for speech and motor function, guided by anesthesiologist monitoring.
vis.caption: Awake craniotomy for functional brain mapping

steps.tx: **Autonomic dysreflexia** affects patients with a cord injury above **T6**, and bladder distension is the commonest trigger. The patient develops headache, sweating and flushing above the level of injury. The team sits the patient up, lowers the legs and drains the **bladder** at once. Treating the trigger matters more than giving drugs alone, although vasodilators may help.
steps.say: A blocked bladder can trigger a dangerous reflex in a patient with high spinal injury. Blood pressure rises sharply while the face becomes flushed and sweaty above the injury. The team sits the patient upright and drains the bladder without any delay. Removing the trigger usually settles the blood pressure within a short time. Drugs that dilate blood vessels help when the trigger cannot be removed quickly.
